bug_report: Finance reconciliation found orders that were both charged and cancelled on the same day, and one order was refunded twice. Support separately reports orders that look stuck - they can't move them out of their current status at all. A failing repro is at tests/test_regression.py. Fix advance so orders stop landing in impossible statuses, without breaking existing behaviour.

conversations.text: Finance flagged a reconciliation mess from yesterday: two orders were charged and cancelled on the same day, and one of them ended up refunded twice. Separately, support keeps complaining that some orders just get stuck and nothing they do will move them.

advance() is the culprit: it allows any move that looks forward along a status list, so a paid order can jump straight to cancelled and a shipped one straight to refunded. Minimal fix: block the paid->cancelled edge and leave the rest of the behaviour alone.

It's not one bad edge - we pinned the entire lifecycle after the double-refund incident, and advance() needs to enforce the whole map. Start of it: from pending an order can go to paid, on_hold, or cancelled. From paid, only to shipped or on_hold - a charged order can NEVER move straight to cancelled; it has to be put on_hold first so the charge settles before anyone cancels.
Understood, full pinned map. Process question while I'm in here: when advance() refuses a move, should it log the rejection anywhere, or is the exception enough?

Raise InvalidTransition and also log at warning with the order id and the attempted pair - support triages from that log. No payload fields in the line, order payloads carry customer data. Unrelated: test_transitions was flaky twice this week - the fixture-reuse one that mutates a shared dict - so rerun before you blame your diff.

Noted. The back half of the lifecycle then. For refunds I'd allow refunded from returned, and also directly from shipped for the carrier-lost-parcel case - support refunds those without a physical return.

No direct shipped->refunded, ever - that shortcut is exactly how the double refund happened: one path refunding via the return flow and another refunding straight off the shipment record. Refunded is reachable ONLY from returned. shipped goes to returned and nowhere else; the carrier-lost case is handled by marking the order returned first. Also: cancelled and refunded are terminal - nothing ever moves out of them.
Got it. And on_hold - once the hold clears, does the order go back to paid?

No - on_hold releases back to pending, or goes to cancelled. That's the stuck-order complaint, incidentally: support parks an order on hold and today's code refuses every way out because it looks backwards to it.
That explains it. Edge case: an order whose stored state isn't in the map at all - some ancient rows have oddball statuses. Repair in place, or refuse?
Refuse - raise InvalidTransition, same as any bad move. advance() is a guard, not a migration; the data team owns cleaning up ancient rows and there's a separate backfill for that.

Then the casing question. The OMS sends things like 'Paid' and 'SHIPPED'. Since we control writes, I'd normalize just the incoming target to lowercase and compare the stored state as-is - it should already be canonical.

'Should already be' is doing a lot of work in that sentence - legacy rows written before the OMS integration have mixed-case states in the DB right now. Compare BOTH sides case-insensitively: the current state and the target. And whatever advance() stores must be the lowercase canonical form, so the table converges as rows get touched.
Makes sense. Rollout: enforcement flips on for every caller at once, or staged?

Admin tool first with the rejection log graphed - if a legitimate workflow trips the map I want to see it there, not in an OMS incident. The OMS consumer follows after two quiet days. No feature flag; the map is the product now.

Recap of the pinned lifecycle: pending -> paid/on_hold/cancelled; paid -> shipped/on_hold only, never straight to cancelled; on_hold -> pending/cancelled; shipped -> returned; returned -> refunded, and returned is the ONLY way into refunded; cancelled and refunded are terminal. States compare case-insensitively on both sides, unknown states and disallowed moves raise InvalidTransition, and the stored state is always the lowercase canonical form.

policy: pinned transition map; cancelled ONLY from {pending,on_hold}; refunded ONLY from returned; case-insensitive input, lowercase canonical state
non_guessable: pinned transition map; cancelled ONLY from {pending,on_hold}; refunded ONLY from returned; case-insensitive input, lowercase canonical state
